title: How Land Diving Works
summary: Josh and Chuck recap their live tour stops (San Francisco, San Diego, Dallas, Austin, New Orleans, Atlanta, Birmingham) and plug an upcoming South by Southwest appearance, then examine land diving (nagol) on Pentecost Island in Vanuatu: the origins in the Tomalie legend, the vine-tied jumps from towers up to about 100 feet, the 1994 and 2006 deaths, the male-only rule, outsider jumpers such as Cal Muller, tourism and filming restrictions, and the ritual's role in ensuring the yam harvest and marking boys' passage to manhood. The episode closes with listener mail from Michael, a doctoral student in Oregon, on non-timber forest products and terminology for developing countries.
topics: Stuff You Should Know tour recap

segments.title: Opening banter and tour recap
segments.summary: Hosts recap their live tour stops in San Francisco, San Diego, Dallas, Austin, New Orleans, Atlanta and Birmingham, plug a South by Southwest appearance and a local band gig, and thank Squarespace for sponsoring the tour.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live tour

segments.title: Origins of land diving on Pentecost Island
segments.summary: Land diving, called nagol, is introduced as an ancient ritual on Pentecost Island in Vanuatu. Hosts discuss its resemblance to bungee jumping, A.J. Hackett's popularization of bungee jumping, and a dispute over intellectual property and tribal rituals.

segments.title: How the jump works: towers, vines, and the yam harvest
segments.summary: Towers up to about 100 feet are built from wood and vines before yam season. The jumpers tie vines to their ankles, fold their arms, and aim to touch the ground with their shoulders. The 1994 death of a jumper in front of Queen Elizabeth and a 2006 fatality are mentioned, and the jump is tied to ensuring a good yam harvest.

segments.title: Legend of Tomalie and the male-only rule
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Tomalie legend, in which a woman escapes an abusive husband by jumping from a tree with vines on her ankles. Versions differ on what followed. Women are not permitted to jump, and outsiders were largely barred, with Cal Muller noted as a rare exception.

segments.title: History of outsiders, tourism, and the ceremony
segments.summary: Missionaries, Irving and Electra Johnson of National Geographic in 1953, and Cal Muller are described as early outside witnesses. The ritual was banned in the late 1800s, revived after World War Two, and became a tourist attraction. Ceremonies are performed on a set day and then weekly. Preparation includes platform construction, a sleepover, and vine selection by an elder.
topics: ritual revival after World War Two

segments.title: Jump day, attire, rite of passage, and filming ban
segments.summary: Jumpers speak from the platform before leaping, and the crowd reacts. Women wear grass skirts and men wear traditional attire. Young boys jump as a rite of passage into manhood after circumcision. The government of Vanuatu restricted filming in 2006 to limit commercialization.

segments.title: Listener mail on non-timber forest products
segments.summary: Listener Michael, a doctoral student in Oregon, notes that non-timber forest products such as mushrooms, berries and roots matter for forest economics. Hosts discuss the terms developing and underdeveloped versus low-income country, and the origin of the term third world.
